title: Tool invocation ergonomics: schema layers, validation semantics, and recovery messages
creator: Nina Patel
description: Define a multi-layer JSON schema approach and runtime validation semantics for tool/function calls that balance strict authoring guarantees with graceful compatibility for older clients and streaming/partial responses. Goal: reduce customer-facing errors, improve debuggability, and enable automatic lightweight recovery behavior for common mistakes (missing optional fields, type coercion, truncated JSON in streaming).
background: We currently accept tool invocation manifests as free-form JSON blobs with ad-hoc validation performed in various runtimes. This causes inconsistent error messages, surprising runtime failures (especially with streaming outputs and when callers use older SDKs), and high support load. Other teams have created temporary shims in SDKs that mask errors but do not provide consistent telemetry or user-facing hints.
proposed_solution: Introduce three schema layers: 1) canonical schema (authoritative, strict types, required/optional annotations, and field deprecation metadata), 2) compatibility shim rules (coercion rules, deprecated-field mappings, renamed fields mapping), and 3) runtime relaxation profile (per-route flags: allow-missing-optional, allow-trailing-commas, streaming-fragment-recovery). Implement a validation pipeline in the runtime: pre-parse -> shim/coerce -> validate -> augment error with actionable hint -> decide outcome (reject / coerce-and-continue / fallback). Standardize error codes and human-friendly messages and expose them through SDKs and Console traces.
acceptance_criteria:
- Canonical schema format spec published (YAML/JSON + field metadata and deprecation mapping)
- Runtime accepts schema and applies compatibility shim rules documented above
- Validation error taxonomy defined with stable error codes and localized message templates
- SDKs display the new friendly error message for at least Node/Python SDKs
- Telemetry emitted for validation failures, coercions, and fallback events
- End-to-end test demonstrating streaming truncation recovery for a common tool call
edge_cases:
- Streaming responses that terminate mid-JSON object (partial KV cache serialized)
- Binary payloads slipped into string fields by legacy clients
- Deeply nested optional arrays with mixed types (int/float/string)
- Conflicting coercions when multiple rules apply (which wins?)
rollout_plan:
1) Spec review and RFC with Platform/SDK teams (1 week)
2) Implement schema loader and validation pipeline behind feature flag (runtime)
3) Opt-in routes for a small set of high-traffic tools and ship Node/Python SDKs with updated error mapping
4) Monitor telemetry for 2 weeks, iterate on coercion heuristics
5) Flip flag and expand to more routes
notes: Keep coercion deterministic and documented; avoid surprises across SDKs.
Prefer explicit migration guidance in deprecation metadata (suggest replacement field + conversion example).
